reasons: Anchor is Sigvatr's verse in which warm blood (bloð, varmt) flows into the sea (ægi). The Greek loci are confirmed: Il. 11.266 has blood still warm (θερμὸν) from a wound, and Od. 9.388 has blood flowing round the hot stake. varmr ~ θερμός is accepted by Kroonen (*gʷʰor-mo-, initial w- irregular), but the blood nouns are renewed, and Lucr. 2.354 calidum is not cognate (formus would be). The warmth of fresh blood is a literal, generic description.

Anchor has words (orð) conveyed (flytia) to ears (eyrna); Ajax 148-149 has λόγους carried (φέρει) into ὦτα. eyra ~ οὖς is cognate, but that is the only element. 'Convey words to someone's ears' is a commonplace, and Latin 'ad aures perferre' is a possible learned model for saga prose.

The Irish was read: a druid says the name (ainm) of the son born tonight (rogenair, annocht) will be heard (docluinfidear) throughout Ireland (Erinn). ainm ~ ὄνομα ~ nā́ma is exact. (ro)cluinethar is from *ḱlew- (Matasović: *kli-nu- > cluin-), so the root matches κλυτόν / śrútyam / śrutáḥ. But the Irish has a future passive verb, not the verbal adjective of the inherited ὄνομα κλυτόν = śrútyaṃ nā́ma pairing. RV 1.103.4d (naming, dadhé, for fame, śrávase) is a comparable context. A plausible continuation of *h1nómn̥ + *ḱlew-, but the Irish is Middle Irish prose, the phrasing is natural, and birth prophecy has Christian models.

The proverb is confirmed in the anchor (eyro) and in Jómsvíkinga s427 (eyru, introduced by mælt). NRA-norrfragm-67 (augu, eyru) comes from a letter in a papal or Roman context, i.e. Latin chancery idiom. Herodotus 1.114.2 and Ar. Ach. 92 have only the king's eye (ὀφθαλμόν). Only eyra ~ οὖς is cognate. The Persian institution of the king's eyes and ears spread through Greek and Latin as a learned and proverbial topos, so the parallel is derivative.

Confirmed: nafn with bera in AM-36-fol 123 (bar), AM-36-fol 1 (báro) and AM-63-fol 53 (bar, tignar); RV 1.103.4b and 5.30.5b (nā́ma, bíbhrat); Eur. Hel. 66 (ὄνομα, φέρω); Soph. OC 60 (φέρουσι, τοὔνομα). Both elements are exactly cognate (*bher- + *h1nómn̥) in the same verb-object relation across three branches. But 'bear a name/title' is a cross-linguistically natural metaphor, and Latin nomen + ferre/gerere offers a learned model for the Norse prose use of titles.

Same anchor as L001 (bloð, varmt); Il. 11.266 (αἷμ̓, θερμὸν, ὠτειλῆς) is confirmed. There is a single cognate adjective (varmr ~ θερμός, Kroonen *gʷʰor-mo-). The blood noun is renewed and the predicate differs (flowing into the sea vs rising from a wound). Literal and generic.

Confirmed: the anchor has sigr eða bana; MBh 6 BhaGī 2.37 (s73), 9.29.25 and 4.64.57 have hato vā / jitvā vā. bani (*gʷʰon-) and hata- (*gʷʰn̥-to-) share a root but differ in morphology and role (object noun 'death' vs participle 'slain'). 'Victory' is not cognate. 'Victory or death' is a universal battle disjunction.

Anchor is Norwegian law: an unborn child inherits if it comes (kǫmr) alive (lifí) into light (líos) and is baptised (skírt). Lucr. 5.224-225 is confirmed (luminis, oras, aluo, profudit). ljós and lūmen share *leuk- but are different derivatives, and the verbs are not cognate. Birth as coming into the light is near-universal. In a legal text tied to baptism, Latin legal and ecclesiastical idiom (in lucem edi, vivus natus) is a likely model.

Confirmed: Il. 24.557 with 24.558 (ζώειν, ὁρᾶν, φάος, ἠελίοιο), a recurrent Homeric formula for being alive, and RV 10.37.7d (jyók, jīvā́ḥ, paśyema, sūrya), plus RV 9.4.6b and 6.52.5b. There are two cognate elements, not one as the lead states: ἠέλιος ~ sū́rya (*seh2wel-) and ζώειν ~ jīvá- (*gʷ(i)eh3- / *gʷih3-wo-, Beekes s.v. βίος). The 'see' verbs are renewed. The figure (life = seeing the sun) is the same, in comparable contexts (a wish or prayer for continued life), with no translation path. Some generic risk, since seeing light is a natural sign of life.

Confirmed: anchor (veria, oddi, egio) and Beo. 1550 (ord, ecge). oddr = ord (*uzda-, Kroonen) and egg = ecg are exact cognates in the same coordinated merism, and the formula is genuinely Common Germanic. But it is intra-branch only (no non-Germanic partner), so it is weak as evidence for PIE phraseology, and 'point and edge' is a near-natural weapon merism.

Confirmed: the skaldic verse has hendi, halda and yfir with Noregs mǫnnom; Il. 9.420 and 24.374 have χεῖρα with ὑπερέσχε(θε). The only cognates are yfir ~ ὑπέρ, a preposition versus a verbal preverb. Neither hǫnd/χείρ nor halda/ἔχω is cognate. Holding one's hand over someone for protection is generic and also biblical.

Confirmed: the anchor (hǫfoðit, kné, svefn); Laxdæla AM-132-fol 174r:28 (hǫfuðit, kné, sofnar); KUB 36.89 rev., where the god is asleep (šuppariyanza) on Tešimi's knees (genuwaš). kné ~ genu- (*ǵonu-) is exact. šupparie- 'sleep' is from *swep- per Kloekhorst (ON svefn cognate). The Hittite noun tešḫa- is not cognate. Two cognate elements in the same scene (sleeping on someone's knees/lap), but the syntax differs (svefn as subject vs a participle), and the scene is a natural bodily posture with basic vocabulary. 'Knee' for lap is pan-IE usage.

Same anchor as L008 (kǫmr, lifí, líos). Lucr. 1.22, 1.179 (effert), 5.224 and 2.617 (uiuam, progeniem, edant), all with luminis + oras, are confirmed, as is Il. 16.188 (φόωσδε, a different root). The *leuk- root is shared, but the derivatives differ (ljós vs lūmen) and the motion verbs are not cognate. The figure is universal, and the Norse legal context points to Latin legal or baptismal idiom.

Confirmed: the skaldic verse (sverþ, bito) and Beo. 1455 (beado-mēcas, bītan) and 1524 (beado-lēoma, bītan). bíta = bītan is exact and the 'weapon bites' idiom is Common Germanic. But it is a single cognate verb, intra-branch only, and the metaphor is easily formed independently (cf. Latin mordere of iron).

Confirmed: the anchor (vacþi, aðrir, sváfo) and Il. 10.1-4 (ἄλλοι, εὗδον, ὕπνῳ, Ἀγαμέμνονα). Only the *swep- root links them, as different parts of speech: sofa is a verb, while Greek uses εὗδον plus the noun ὕπνος. aðrir (*anþera-) and ἄλλοι (*h2elyo-) are not cognate. 'The leader wakes while the others sleep' is a generic narrative device, and the contexts differ.

Confirmed: Xen. Cyr. 8.2.11 (βασιλέως, ὀφθαλμοὶ, ὦτα) and 8.2.12 (πολλὰ, βασιλέως, ὦτα), and the anchor (morg, konongs, eyro). The match is close, but only eyra ~ οὖς is cognate. The king's many ears and eyes is a Persian institution that passed into the Greek and Latin learned and proverbial tradition, a plausible source for a medieval Norse proverb (introduced by mælt). Derivative, not inherited.
